name: Bates method eye exercises

lead: The Bates method is a set of eye relaxation and eye-movement exercises devised by the New York eye physician William Horatio Bates (1860-1931). It is promoted as a way to improve eyesight without glasses. In looksmaxxing circles it appears in the fringe category, where some people say eye exercises can change how the eyes look or function.

Bates held that focusing errors come from mental strain on the muscles around the eyeball, and that relaxation could reverse them. Mainstream ophthalmology and optometry reject that explanation of how the eye focuses, and published reviews have not found that eye exercises objectively improve visual acuity.

paras: Bates proposed that the external muscles of the eyeball, not the lens, change the eye's shape to focus, and that tension from mental strain causes myopia and other conditions. His techniques include palming (covering closed eyes with the palms), visualising dark objects, shifting and swinging the gaze, and sunning (exposing the eyes or closed lids to sunlight). Vision scientists attribute focusing to the ciliary muscle and lens, and explain apparent improvements as adaptation to blur or better interpretation of blurry images.

Reviews by ophthalmology bodies have found no objective improvement in eyesight from eye exercises. Critics have raised safety concerns, including driving or working without needed lenses, delaying treatment of conditions such as glaucoma or childhood amblyopia, and retinal or skin damage from looking toward the sun. The method is not a regulated medical treatment, and marketers of some Bates-derived programmes have faced legal action.

lead: The Bates method is a system of eye relaxation and eye-movement exercises developed by the American eye physician William Horatio Bates (1860-1931) and promoted as a way to improve eyesight without corrective lenses.[1] Bates published his main statement of the method in 1920 in a book titled The Cure of Imperfect Sight by Treatment Without Glasses, also issued as Perfect Sight Without Glasses.[1]

Bates held that the muscles surrounding the eyeball change its shape to focus, that refractive errors and several other eye conditions arise from mental strain on those muscles, and that relaxation can relieve them.[1] Mainstream eye care holds a different account of focusing, in which the ciliary muscle changes the shape of the lens.[1] A 2013 paper in Ophthalmic and Physiological Optics discussed how the Bates method and other proposed myopia cures are claimed to work and why people report benefits.[2]

A 2004 review by the American Academy of Ophthalmology found no evidence that eye exercises objectively improve eyesight, and a 2005 review of 43 studies from Christchurch Hospital reached a similar conclusion for visual acuity, according to Wikipedia.[1] In looksmaxxing communities the method is sometimes mentioned alongside other fringe suggestions that eye exercises can alter eye function or appearance.

paras: Bates proposed that normal sight depends on relaxed use of the eyes and mind, and that habitual strain produces blurred vision. He considered glasses to be "eye crutches" and advised followers to stop wearing them.[1] The method is a set of practices rather than a device or product.[3]

Palming involves closing the eyes and covering them with the palms without pressing on the eyeballs. Bates reported that patients saw lights and colours while palming and attributed this to strain, whereas skeptics attribute it to the brain's background visual activity in darkness.[1]

Visualisation involves imagining black or dark letters and objects, which Bates treated as a gauge of relaxation. Shifting and swinging involve moving the gaze back and forth to create an impression of moving objects; later promoters simplified these into up-down, side-to-side and near-far gaze changes.[1]

Sunning involves exposing the eyes to sunlight. Bates later advised exposing closed eyelids for longer periods and the open white of the eye only briefly.[1] Grokipedia describes central fixation, swinging, palming, sunning and shifting as core elements.[3]

Bates published an article in 1891 reporting that he had reversed seven cases of myopia, and in 1911 he reported teaching myopic schoolchildren to focus at a distance.[1] In 1917 he partnered with the physical-culture promoter Bernarr Macfadden on a correspondence course that the American Medical Association's Bureau of Investigation criticised; Bates's name was later dropped and the course renamed.[1] Bates began publishing the magazine Better Eyesight in July 1919.[1][3]

In 1929 the Federal Trade Commission filed a complaint against Bates over advertising. He died in 1931, after which his widow Emily Lierman Bates and other associates continued to teach the method.[1] In 1932 Gayelord Hauser published a book that endorsed the method and added his own exercises and dietary products.[1]

Margaret Darst Corbett taught the method at her School of Eye Education in Los Angeles. In late 1940 she and an assistant were charged under California's Medical Practice Act for treating eyes without a license; Corbett was found not guilty.[1] The writer Aldous Huxley, who had severely impaired vision after keratitis, took lessons from Corbett in 1939 and described his experience in The Art of Seeing (1942), claiming his vision was roughly twice as good as when he wore glasses. Ophthalmologists including Stewart Duke-Elder and Walter B. Lancaster suggested his vision had fluctuated naturally or that he had learned to use it better.[1]

The American Academy of Ophthalmology reviewed visual training in 2004 and found no evidence that eye exercises objectively improve eyesight, attributing apparent gains to factors such as better interpretation of blurred images or a pinhole effect.[1] A 2005 review by Rawstron and colleagues at Christchurch Hospital covered 43 studies and found no clear scientific evidence supporting eye exercises for visual acuity.[1]

Writers on blur adaptation, including Elliott (2013), Khan (2013) and Cufflin and Mallen (2020), describe how the visual system adapts when lenses are removed, which can make vision seem better.[1] Wikipedia notes that Bates's own photographs, offered as evidence that image size does not change during focusing, were judged by the optometrist Philip Pollack in 1956 to be too blurred to support that conclusion, and that measured elongation of the eye during accommodation is far too small to account for Bates's claims.[1]
Eye-care bodies cited by Grokipedia state that exercises can help in specific eye-muscle conditions such as strabismus but do not change the optical structure of the eye.[3]

Critics have said that discarding or underusing glasses can be dangerous while driving, that followers may delay treatment for conditions such as glaucoma or childhood amblyopia, and that gazing at the sun risks photic retinopathy and eyelid skin damage, which Bates described as "always temporary."[1] The philosopher Frank J. Leavitt argued that because the method depends on relaxation and imagination it is hard to test with placebo controls.[1]

Practitioners of "natural vision correction," many without medical or optometric credentials, continue to market Bates-based programmes, sometimes combined with vision therapy.[1] The heavily advertised See Clearly Method, which adapted palming and light therapy, was halted by a court order in November 2006 over dishonest marketing.[1]

Trials specific to the Bates method are few. A small clinical study published in the Ayurvedic journal Ayu in 2012 evaluated a yoga eye practice (Trataka) and eye exercises for refractive error and presbyopia in an Ayurvedic framework; it is a study of related eye exercises, not of the Bates method itself.[4] Broader reviews of eye exercises, including the 2004 American Academy of Ophthalmology review and a 2005 Christchurch Hospital review of 43 studies, found no clear evidence of objective visual-acuity improvement.[1] Historical optometry and ophthalmology papers from 1952 to 1975 discussed Bates's ideas, including a 1952 optometry paper on 'flashes of clear vision' and a 1975 biographical article on Bates.[5][6]

lore.intro: In online appearance and wellness communities the Bates method is mentioned as a drug-free way to improve eyesight or eye function, and occasionally in connection with eye appearance.[3]

claims.claim: Eye relaxation exercises like palming can improve eyesight and reduce myopia without glasses.
Glasses weaken the eyes and cause dependency.
Sunning (exposing the eyes to sunlight) strengthens the eyes.
The eyeball changes shape through the external eye muscles to focus, rather than the lens.
